hypothesis: In real sunflower capitula, the two families of contact-parastichy spirals cross at angles that are roughly constant across the disc (isogonal), and the crossing angles cluster away from 90° instead of being mostly orthogonal.
pass_criterion: From seed or floret centre coordinates in at least 20 capitula, fit a logarithmic spiral to each parastichy family. The claim passes if both conditions hold. (a) Within each capitulum, the crossing angle between the two families, measured at floret positions from r=0.3R to R, has a coefficient of variation below 10%. (b) Fewer than 25% of capitula have a mean crossing angle within 90±5°, and the pooled mean crossing angle differs from 90° by more than 5°.
fail_criterion: The claim fails if either of two things holds. (a) The within-capitulum coefficient of variation of the crossing angle is 20% or more in most capitula, so the intersection is not isogonal. (b) At least 50% of capitula have a mean crossing angle within 90±5°, so orthogonal crossing is common rather than rare.
interpretation: Thompson's 'spirals' are the visible contact parastichies, the 21/34, 34/55 or 55/89 families. 'Isogonal' means a constant crossing angle, as for logarithmic spirals about a common pole. 'Orthogonal' means a crossing angle of 90°, which Church's model required. Both are measured as the angle between the tangents of the two fitted spiral families at each floret. The test is limited to the scope of the quote, which is sunflower capitula. The modern reinterpretation is that real discs follow Vogel-type golden-angle packing, which gives roughly Fibonacci parastichies with crossing angles near 90° only in the central region. Parastichies are not exact logarithmic spirals, so 'constant' is tested with a tolerance and not as an exact identity.
no_dataset_reason: I could not identify a public, citable dataset of sunflower (Helianthus annuus) capitulum floret or seed coordinates, or of parastichy crossing angles, whose landing page and DOI I could confirm. The portals I know well (GBIF, NCBI, MorphoSource, Dryad, and others) hold occurrence records, sequences or trait tables, not per-floret geometry of sunflower discs. Naming a dataset I cannot verify would break the no-fabrication rule. The test would need a new measurement set from high-resolution capitulum photographs or scans, or a Dryad or Zenodo deposit of floret coordinates if one exists.
